In the latter half of the 19th century, Chelsea went from being a bucolic suburb to an industrialized city neighborhood, with smoke-belching factories lining the Hudson River, including a former Nabisco production facility, which is now Chelsea Market. Today, its attractions remain numerous, including bustling 14th Street to the south, the twisting elevated path of the High Line running like the neighborhood’s backbone, the Fashion Institute of Technology, and the boutique hotels and art galleries serving as a buffer between residential Chelsea and the Hudson River. The precise borders are controversial, but for the purposes of this map, the neighborhood runs from around Sixth Avenue on the east to the Hudson River on the west and from 14th Street on the south to 30th Street on the north.

What’s changed in this update: We’ve added Markette and Konban; we’ve removed Ddobar by Joomak, Swagat, and Rangoon (all three have closed), along with Sullivan Street Bakery and Portale.

On the western edge of Chelsea, find Hav & Mar, a restaurant from Marcus Samuelsson. Handily merging the food of Sweden, Ethiopia, and New York, he and chef-partner Fariyal Abdullahi present an array of unlikely dishes, including the Addis York — his version of Ethiopian doro wat — featuring glazed chicken drumsticks triumphantly pointing skyward. The bread basket alone is worth the visit.

Before the current mania for Italian authenticity swept over the city, lots of cured pork products, such as guanciale and lardo, were tough to find unless you dropped by this Chelsea deli. These days, this over-100-year-old pork store mounts a steam table full of red-sauce pastas at lunchtime, plus a menu of giant hero sandwiches.

This Chelsea restaurant comes from chef India Doris as a reflection of herself and her culinary background, which means modern European dishes with Caribbean touches for dinner — don’t miss the peri peri chicken (an ode to Nando’s) and the braised oxtail gratin. Check out the downstairs cocktail bar, the Argyle, if you’ve got time.

After a several-year hiatus, Txikito returned to Chelsea with a bang in 2022, still peddling Basque small plates of octopus, olive oil-poached cod, beef cheek and jowl, and king oyster mushroom carpaccio for dinner. The chefs are the wife-and-husband team of Alex Raij and Eder Montero, and the premises recall a Spanish tapas bar in style, intimacy, and good smells.

Hey Yuet serves Cantonese dim sum and dishes from Hong Kong. From classic har gow to char siu bao, some of the best dim sum in town is to be found here all day and into the night.

This railroad-car diner vastly extends the diner food genre to accommodate many international dishes from a modern perspective. Sure, there are lavish breakfasts and a memorable fried chicken, but there’s also tuna tartare, rye pancakes, and tuna nicoise.

Ayesha Nurdjaja’s Eastern Mediterranean follow-up to Shuka still packs people in, here for the lively bar scene and excellent menu of dips, breads, braised and grilled meats, and vegetables. Dishes wear bold flavors, thanks to fistfuls of fresh herbs, and details like harissa, pickles, za’atar, or citrus. Go with a crowd to try more, but if it’s peak dining hour, be prepared: It’s loud.

This homey Italian restaurant on the edge of Chelsea’s gallery district makes a nice refuge after an afternoon of art-hopping. Founded in 1997, it used to be part of a chain specializing in discount pastas whipped up on the spot, and part of that aura remains, though the menu now concentrates on antipasti, panini, and pizzas, with the occasional risotto or lasagna thrown in for good measure.

Located in one of Chelsea’s quieter sections surrounded by distinguished older buildings, Cookshop was founded with a farm-to-table ethos in 2005 and has gradually grown to be a favorite spot for a tumultuous brunch or a quiet dinner. Vegetables are emphasized — even in its inventive pizzas — and there’s a substantial commitment to seafood, while many appetizers and entrees are prepared in a wood-fired oven.

Occupying an elegant townhouse in western Chelsea, Qanoon serves distinguished Palestinian food. Many of the mezze have rarely been produced so well in this area, including muhammara, hummus, baba ghanoush, and labneh configured as orbs for dipping. Main dishes are complete dinners, best of which is makloubeh, a lamb and eggplant casserole.
